Prepare authentication219 repetitions

Use the same count on both devices for a predictable test. The proof uses at least the key holder’s minimum and the verifier’s request. Smaller counts are useful for development; the nominal repetition bound is not a security guarantee for this experimental circuit.

Each attempt has a fixed deadline selected above; transport adjustments do not extend it. The 8 × 8, 16-round neural circuit runs in a worker. Reset discards this device’s key and pairing state; reset the other device too before trying again.

This screen → other device’s cameraLocal outgoing QR settings

Set each device independently, regardless of its authentication role. A phone usually needs smaller, simpler QRs for the computer’s webcam. The incoming QR size is chosen on the other device.

Adaptation can reduce outgoing chunk size after repeated missing ACKs, then cautiously increase it for later messages up to your configured limit. It does not change the proof or incoming settings. ACKs stay compact and use Q correction.

Settings are ready for the next attempt.

You can apply settings during an attempt. Smaller chunks restart only the current message, preserving the proof. Larger chunks and window changes take effect on the next message; display timing and ACK hold change immediately.

The device ID is a local label, not a credential. Keys exist only for this page session and are discarded by reset or reload. This attempt authenticates the key holder to the verifier; the key holder’s result is a peer report, not proof of the verifier’s identity. Swap roles for a separate reverse-direction test.

Reports contain settings, timings, and public fingerprints; never secret keys or proof bytes.
Light is the link. Bytes are the proof.
